ratings.rationale: Postulated software tampering of A3.1 by a ground intruder. Wrong grouping creates ghost or lost tracks (Deception, Denial). Central module, so whole coverage is affected. Inconsistent residuals are likely caught by the monitor in a strong pass; otherwise ghost tracks show only at ATM.
ratings.issue: No mechanism or source. Generic code compromise of one module, subsumed by T3.12 and overlapping T3.04. The vector is too vague to separate it from platform compromise.

ratings.rationale: Altering monitor or cross-check logic gives wrong verdicts: missed discrepancies or false flags (Deception). Postulated, needs ground code access. Affects the whole constellation. The checks are the detector, so only software or audit integrity at L4 would reveal it.
ratings.issue: Overlaps T3.06, since a threshold change is a special case, and T3.12. 'Pass or fail wrongly' mixes two goals. Only A3.4 is named but the cross-check A3.5 is also in scope.

ratings.rationale: Write access to the ephemeris and clock-state store creates a bias equivalent to a clock offset, giving displacement if undetected. Postulated, T2 intruder. The monitor catches a large single-satellite bias in a strong pass; a weak pass leaves the stealth window unchecked.
ratings.issue: Store tampering is not a true onboard time offset and ephemeris errors are not temporal, so tau is doubtful. A3.3 is only the consumer. Overlaps T3.04 and the upstream A4.2 path.

ratings.rationale: Process-level modification of solver inputs after association biases the observables directly. Displacement with a nominal annotation if the bias is inside the stealth window. Postulated, needs ground host access. A strong pass catches large single-satellite bias; a weak pass does not.
ratings.issue: Same effect as T3.03 and a consequence of host compromise (T3.12), distinguished only by where the tampering happens. Consider merging. No mechanism or source.

ratings.rationale: Exhausting the central solver denies solutions to all users in coverage, so regional denial. Source #65 is a non-peer-reviewed talk on space vulnerabilities, not solver-specific, so treated as analogue theory. Latency or queue monitoring at L3 would detect it.
ratings.issue: RF flooding saturates payload or downlink before the solver, and crafted reports need link access, so entry layer and adversary are ambiguous. Two vectors are mixed in one record.

ratings.rationale: Raising detection thresholds widens the stealth window for every route and has no target-report effect by itself, so it is an enabler. Threshold masters sit in A4.4 and are changed through channel C. Visible only through configuration audit at L4; a weak pass hides any bias in the window.
ratings.issue: Entry asset is A4.4 at L4, not A3.4 or A3.5, which only apply the thresholds. Overlaps T3.02. GNSS-PTP conformance thresholds of A4.1 are a sibling case not covered.

ratings.rationale: Synchronised emitters make the independent and broadcast positions agree, so a fabricated target is annotated verified. Support comes from terrestrial multilateration spoofing work, hence analogue. Consistent multi-source emissions pass L3 checks; only external correlation at ATM may reveal it.
ratings.issue: Entry is the air interface at L1 and the cross-check is only the defeated defence, so this is largely multi-emitter spoofing viewed at L3. Source #6 is a countermeasure paper, not attack evidence.

ratings.rationale: Perturbing one of two independent positions of an honest aircraft makes the cross-check flag a genuine target, which is a wrong integrity verdict (Deception). Cited work is terrestrial and simulated or countermeasure oriented. The flag is raised at L3; its cause is not identifiable.
ratings.issue: Defined by its goal, not a mechanism: the perturbation route (aircraft GNSS spoofing or local RF) is unstated. Impact is mostly nuisance, so Damage 4 is arguable. Neither cited source shows this attack.

ratings.rationale: Tampering at the encoder lets a real aircraft be shown wrongly with a nominal integrity flag, downstream of every L3 predicate. Postulated, needs ground code access. All reports are affected. Only ATM-side cross-checks or controller correlation could notice.
ratings.issue: No mechanism or source. Generic code compromise, overlapping T3.12 and the data-feed asset A4.5. Whether ASTERIX output integrity is monitored downstream is not stated.

ratings.rationale: Read access to track stores or reports discloses movements. This reaches disclosure only, so Damage 1. Postulated, needs intrusion or insider access. Passive reading is visible only through access auditing at L4.
ratings.issue: ADS-B-derived tracks are largely public, so the confidentiality value is limited to non-public annotations or filtered traffic. Tracks sit in A3.3, not only A3.6. Low risk by design.

ratings.rationale: Altering or suppressing logs degrades attribution and has no effect on a target report, so it is a classic enabler (Repudiation). Source #65 is a non-peer-reviewed talk I could not assess, so evidence is treated as theoretical analogue. Detectable only by log-integrity audit at L4.
ratings.issue: Audit logs are hosted in A4.8 at L4, not in A3.3. Overlaps T3.12 since log control follows from host control. The cited talk's relevance to log tampering is unclear.

ratings.rationale: Control of the host gives control of every module, so all goal classes are reachable. Ground-segment IT compromise is documented in other satellite networks (analogue); #65 not assessed. Host control can disable L3 checks, so detection depends on L4 security monitoring.
ratings.issue: Parent threat of T3.01 to T3.11; those records are largely its consequences, so counting them separately risks double counting. 'Remote exploitation' covers several distinct entry vectors.

missing_threats.title: CPS time-reference corruption
missing_threats.why: Offset of the ground host time base used for stamping, association and ephemeris propagation; not covered although the timing dependency is central.

missing_threats.title: Forced weak geometry
missing_threats.why: Selective denial or suppression of receptions to push HDOP above h*, opening the stealth window for another attack.

missing_threats.title: Stale or replayed report acceptance
missing_threats.why: Association time-window handling may accept delayed or replayed unauthenticated reports (W4); no L3 replay-handling threat is listed.

missing_threats.title: Ground software supply-chain compromise
missing_threats.why: Trojanised updates or dependencies reach L3 modules by a route other than remote exploitation.

missing_threats.title: Solver and tracker model-parameter poisoning
missing_threats.why: EKF/IMM noise and gating parameters altered to mask or induce track errors; distinct from threshold relaxation.

rubric_ambiguities: Enabler vs Deception: a tampered verdict logic both changes integrity verdicts on reports and masks other attacks; the rubric does not say which wins.
Affected users A for a compromised central module: whole constellation, or only the aircraft actually touched?
Di for threats outside the monitor chain, such as encoder tampering or log tampering: L4 or 5 when no check exists by design.
Evidence level when the only cited source is a non-peer-reviewed talk of unclear content, and the analogue-only rule for generic IT compromise.
Entry layer when a record's asset sits at L3 but the controlling asset or the attacker's entry (L1 RF, L4 configuration) is in another layer.
batch_comments.overall: Mostly postulated, uncited L3 records. Many are consequences of host compromise (T3.12) or share an effect with T3.03 and T3.04, so the catalogue risks double counting. T3.07 and T3.08 are really L1-entry threats. T3.06 belongs at L4. Several records need a mechanism and sources.
